title: Beautiful patience
hookLine: losing Joseph, Jacob says: patience is most fitting, a beautiful patience
carry: his eyes go white with grief
last: WHO COULD BE BETTER THAN HIM.

cards: Evening. A group of brothers comes home crying, carrying their little brother's shirt. There's blood on it.
A wolf took him, they say, while we were racing and left him with our things. Their father, Jacob, holds the shirt. In the Quran's telling, he doesn't believe them.
The blood is false, and somehow he knows it. His favorite son is gone, the ones in front of him are lying, and he has to answer right there, in that room.
The twelfth chapter of the Quran, the chapter of Joseph, gives his answer in two Arabic words.

teach.b: First, the words. Jacob tells his sons that their own souls have talked them into something. And then: sabrun jamil.
Not grim patience, not gritted teeth. And he adds: it is God whose help is sought against what you describe. He doesn't shout, and he doesn't pretend to believe them.
Second, what it isn't. Beautiful patience is not dry-eyed. Later in the chapter, when another son is lost, Jacob says the same two words again.
Then he turns away and says, alas for Joseph, and his eyes go white with grief. In the Quran, a patient man's grief is plain to see.
Third, where the complaint goes. When his sons tell him to stop dwelling on Joseph, Jacob answers that he complains of his grief and sorrow only to God, and knows from God what they don't.
Some commentators describe beautiful patience in just these terms: grief carried to God, without bitterness poured out on the people around you.
He sends his sons to search for Joseph, and tells them not to despair of God's mercy. Fourth, the shape of it. Sabr, from two days ago, met the first blow.
Beautiful patience is the long version: a long separation, with grief, honesty and hope, and without turning the hurt into a weapon. The story, in the end, gives Joseph back.
But Jacob chose his patience long before he knew that.

how: Some Muslims say sabrun jamil, beautiful patience, to one another in long trials, and the story of Jacob and Joseph in the twelfth surah is told as a lesson in it.

o: patience that hides all grief behind a calm face
patience kept only until the truth comes out
patience that grieves and takes its complaint to God

games.q: what's inside Jacob's patience — tap the pairs.

s: in the Quran, Jacob's beautiful patience means he shows no grief
his eyes go white with grief, and he still calls it patience.
Jacob says the same two words on two different losses
on losing Joseph, and again when another son is lost.
Jacob believes the brothers' story about the wolf
he says their souls have talked them into something.

games.q: you're Jacob. your sons hand you a bloodied shirt and a story you don't believe. what do you say?
o: accuse them and send them away.
pretend to believe them, to keep the peace.
name the lie, choose beautiful patience, and seek God's help.
games.why: Jacob tells them their souls have tempted them, then says: sabrun jamil, and God's help is sought.

practice: Find one situation you're having to be patient with, a person who hurt you, a wait that won't end, and notice whether the patience has an edge: a sigh, a story you keep telling about who's to blame.

Let the hurt be fully there, and let the edge soften on each out-breath. If you pray, you can bring the complaint to God the way Jacob did; if not, simply set it down, out of reach of anyone you might aim it at.

wordCard.voice: Beautiful patience: sabrun jamil, Jacob's words in the Quran on losing Joseph. Patience that grieves, and takes its complaint to God. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: his eyes go white with grief. In this story, patience still weeps. Until tomorrow.
